# Conclusions

Schools socialize students into beliefs about meritocracy, promoting effort and talent as the legitimate basis of reward while simultaneously exposing students to the weight of family resources and social connections in shaping outcomes [@resh_sense_2014; @traini_stratification_2022; @goudeau_hidden_2017a]. Students navigate this tension by holding both orientations at once, endorsing merit as an ideal while recognizing that privilege structures actual outcomes, a configuration that can be associated to the concept of _dual consciousness_ [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025; @kluegel_beliefs_1987]. Capturing this complexity requires studies and instruments that distinguish how students perceive meritocracy to work from how they prefer it should work, and that treat merit and privilege as potentially coexisting rather than mutually exclusive, a standard most available measures do not meet. Extending Castillo et al.'s [-@castillo_multidimensional_2023]  multidimensional framework to adolescents, this study tested whether students distinguish merit from privilege and perceptions ("what is") from preferences ("what should be"), using panel survey data from two Chilean students cohorts (8th and 10th graders) across two waves (2023-2024), and whether these dimensions are stable over time and comparable across school stages. The contribution is a modest but foundational one: to establish whether meritocratic beliefs can be measured reliably and equivalently in school-aged populations, as a precondition for studying their developmental trajectory and educational implications (such as for instance gender and/or social class differences) in future studies.

Although this study draws on a single country, its contributions carry implications beyond the Chilean case. Three findings are likely to travel across educational systems. First, the conceptual distinction between perceived and preferred meritocracy, and between meritocratic and privilege-based principles, reflects general cognitive and normative capacities that develop during adolescence regardless of national context; further studies should hel state whether the four-factor structure is able to replicate in other societies. Second, the coexistence of merit endorsement and recognition of privilege, the core pattern underlying dual consciousness, has been documented in China [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025], the United States and Finland [@zhu_meritocratic_2025], and Europe [@kwon_multidimensionality_2024], suggesting it is not a Chilean peculiarity. Third, the logic of longitudinal invariance testing as a prerequisite for developmental inference is methodologically general and applies to any panel study of meritocratic beliefs. By contrast, the specific pattern of cross-cohort non-invariance, concentrated in preferred effort, may be more system-dependent: it likely reflects the particular intensity and timing of school-based sorting in Chile's tracked and marketized system [@madariaga_three_2020; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2013]. Future research in countries with different tracking regimes and stratification profiles will help clarify which aspects of measurement equivalence are universal and which are conditioned by institutional features.

This study has several limitations that also point to directions for future research. First, the measurement scale relies on two items per factor, which restricts both content coverage and reliability; inferences about fine-grained distinctions within dimensions should therefore be drawn with caution. Second, the design comprises only two waves and two school levels. Additional waves and a broader age range are needed to trace developmental trajectories more precisely and to establish when the meaning students attach to meritocracy begins to shift. Third, and most consequentially, the lack of measurement invariance across school cohorts indicates that meritocracy scales cannot be assumed to function equivalently between educational stages. Future studies should therefore examine differential item functioning, develop stage-sensitive item formulations, and adopt partial-invariance approaches to establish comparability [@putnick_measurement_2016; @vandeschoot_checklist_2012]. Addressing these issues would, in turn, allow for a more rigorous examination of substantively meaningful group differences, such as the gender differences in the endorsement of meritocratic beliefs suggested by @gogescu_meritocracy_2025 and @khan_saying_2013. Furthermore, it would also make it possible to examine how beliefs about merit and privilege relate to the school outcomes for which they are likely to matter most: students’ sense of justice and fairness, civic attitudes and engagement, perceptions of school climate, and wellbeing, in addition to academic motivation.
